info.name: Bank Microservices — Customers & Accounts
info.description:
Endpoint tests for the two microservices of the technical test.

**Order matters.** The folders are numbered and chain through collection variables: `01 · Customers` stores `{{customerId}}`, `02 · Accounts` stores `{{accountNumber}}`, `03 · Movements` stores `{{movementId}}`. Running the whole collection top to bottom (Postman Runner or Newman) exercises the happy path, every error code of the contract and the business rules F2/F3, then leaves the database clean.

**Before running:** start both services (`docker compose up --build`) and check `00 · Health`.

**Variables** — defaults point at the ports published by docker-compose:
- `customersUrl` = http://localhost:8081/api/v1
- `accountsUrl` = http://localhost:8082/api/v1

Every request carries assertions, so the collection also runs headless:
`newman run postman/bank-microservices.postman_collection.json`

item.name: 00 · Health
item.description: Actuator of both services. Run these first: if they do not answer, nothing else will.

item.name: 01 · Customers
item.description: CRUD of the customer microservice (port 8081). The POST stores the customer id in the {{customerId}} collection variable, which every later request reuses.

request.description: Inserts the person row and the customer row in a single transaction. `status` defaults to true when omitted; `password` is writeOnly, so it never comes back.

exec: pm.test("id is a UUID assigned by the server", function () {
pm.test("Location header points at the new resource", function () {

request.description: Same identification as the previous request. The unique constraint uq_person_identification is enforced by CustomerService and surfaces as a 409.

exec: pm.test("error body follows the contract", function () {
pm.test("returns the customer that was created", function () {

request.description: The three query params are optional. page defaults to 0 and size to 20; a size outside 1..100 is rejected with a 400.
The contract caps size at 100. Validation stops before the database is queried.
PUT replaces every editable field; `password` is required by the contract, so it always travels. The id and createdAt survive untouched.

exec: pm.test("fields were replaced, id kept", function () {

request.description: Absent fields keep their current value. Only the phone changes here.

exec: pm.test("only the sent field changed", function () {
pm.test("error body follows the contract", function () {

item.name: 02 · Accounts
item.description: CRUD of the account microservice (port 8082). Creating an account validates the customerId over REST against ms-customers, so 01 · Customers has to run first.

request.description: accountNumber is readOnly: the server generates it and ignores any value sent in the body. A freshly created account has availableBalance == initialBalance.

exec: pm.test("server assigned the account number", function () {
pm.test("available balance starts at the initial balance", function () {

request.description: The inter-service call answers 404, so no account is created. If ms-customers were down instead, the answer would be a 502.

exec: pm.test("every row belongs to the customer", function () {

request.description: initialBalance is not part of the update contract: mutating it would unbalance the movement history. Editing an account never touches its available balance.

exec: pm.test("only the sent field changed", function () {

item.name: 03 · Movements
item.description: Rules F2 (a debit subtracts, a credit adds, the value must be greater than zero) and F3 ("Saldo no disponible"). Runs against the account created in 02.

request.description: Rule F2: a credit adds to the balance. The response balance is the account balance AFTER applying the movement — a frozen historical value.

exec: pm.test("credit added to the balance: 1000 + 500", function () {
pm.test("server assigned id and date", function () {

request.description: Rule F2: a debit subtracts. It chains on the balance of the previous movement, not on the initial balance.

exec: pm.test("debit subtracted from the running balance: 1500 - 200", function () {

request.description: Rule F3. The message is the literal text required by the specification. The rejection leaves the database untouched: no movement row, no balance change.

exec: pm.test("literal message required by the specification", function () {
pm.test("no internal detail leaks into the body", function () {

request.description: Rule F2, strict: zero is rejected too. It is a 400 and not a 422 because the request is refused without ever looking at the state of the account.

exec: pm.test("returns the last movement created", function () {

item.name: GET /movements — filter by customer and date range

request.description: Point 5 of the specification: movements by date and by customer. The four filters are optional; the final day of the range is covered in full.

exec: pm.test("returns the movements of the account", function () {

request.description: Only the last movement of an account can be edited: every balance is historical and touching one in the middle would unbalance the chain. The edit applies the delta (new - old): -300 - (-200) = -100 over 1300.

exec: pm.test("balance recomposed by the delta: 1300 - 100", function () {

request.description: The partial branch goes through the same balance door as the PUT: -250 - (-300) = +50 over 1200.
Deleting applies the opposite sign, returning the account to the balance it held before. Reverting a credit lowers the balance, so a delete honours F3 as well.

item.name: 04 · Reports
item.description: Account statement: the only endpoint combining our own data (accounts + movements) with data fetched over REST from the customer microservice.

request.description: Both dates are optional: without startDate the range starts open, without endDate it ends today. The report always states the period it covers.

exec: pm.test("carries the customer fetched from ms-customers", function () {
pm.test("carries the accounts with their movements", function () {

request.description: The contract folds both cases under the same 404: the customer does not exist, or it exists but has no accounts.

item.name: 05 · Teardown
item.description: Leaves the database as it was found. The account can only be deleted once its balance is zero, which is the last business rule left to exercise.

request.description: The account still holds money, so it cannot be deleted. It is a 409 and not a 404: the resource exists, it is its state that blocks the operation.
Exact boundary of rule F3: a NEGATIVE balance is rejected, zero is accepted.

exec: pm.test("balance lands exactly on zero", function () {

request.description: With a zero balance the deletion goes through. It removes the movements of the account first, explicitly, rather than relying on the database cascade.
Deleting the customer also removes its person row (JOINED inheritance, FK ON DELETE CASCADE).
